title: Revenue: when is it recognised?
subtitle: Accrual vs cash - two different views of the same transaction
openingQuestion: You sell goods on day 1, the customer pays on day 30. When is revenue recognised?
openingOptions: Day 30, when the cash actually arrives
Split evenly across the two days
The day the contract is signed
Day 1, when the goods are delivered
explanation: Revenue is recognised when the business has fulfilled its obligation - delivered the goods or completed the service - not when the customer pays. This is the accrual principle, and it exists so profit reflects the period the business activity actually happened in. The cost is a gap between revenue and real cash, which is where accounts receivable lives, and also where a business can show a beautiful income statement while its bank account is nearly empty.

diagram.label: Revenue recognised right at this point
Cash arrives later - becomes a receivable while waiting

realWorldExample.description: Amazon recognises sales revenue as soon as the product is delivered to the customer, even though many customers pay later by credit card - the actual cash flow usually arrives a few days after revenue is recognised.

quiz.question: "Revenue recognition" under modern standards means what?
options: When the contract is signed by both parties and takes effect
When the customer confirms they are satisfied with the product
When the company has completed its delivery/service obligation
When the company has received the full cash payment from the customer
quiz.explanation: Modern standards don't wait for cash. Revenue is recognised once the company has performed its side of the deal (the performance obligation is complete) and believes it will be paid.

quiz.question: Why can a company report high revenue but a low cash count?
options: Because the accounting team made a calculation error somewhere in preparing the report
Because the sales staff weren't paid their salaries on time as required
Because part of the company's money was lost during a bank transfer
Because the company recognises revenue from credit sales before receiving the cash
quiz.explanation: Revenue is recognised as soon as a sale happens (including on credit), but the cash may arrive weeks or months later. The income statement and the cash flow statement will differ.

quiz.question: What is "deferred revenue"?
options: Cash received in advance but delivery not yet completed
Revenue whose recognition is postponed to next year to reduce tax
Revenue already recognised but the customer hasn't paid yet
The portion of revenue cancelled because a customer returned goods
quiz.explanation: The customer pays upfront (for example, an annual software subscription), but the company hasn't delivered the full year's service yet. This cash is a liability, not revenue, until the company performs.

quiz.question: A customer buys online and pays by credit card. When should the company recognise revenue?
options: When the credit card charge succeeds
When the goods are handed to the carrier for shipping
When the customer clicks the order button on the website
When the 30-day return window expires
quiz.explanation: Revenue is recognised when the company completes its part (handing goods to the carrier means delivery is now assured). It doesn't wait for the customer to receive the goods or for cash to hit the account.

quiz.question: A customer can return goods within 30 days. How much revenue should the company recognise?
options: None at all until the 30-day window expires
The full revenue, adjusted later if there are returns
Revenue minus the estimated amount expected to be returned
Only the cash portion already actually received from the customer
quiz.explanation: The company must estimate expected returns based on experience, then only recognise the revenue that is reasonably certain. The uncertain portion is left for after the return window closes.

quiz.question: A company sells a 3-year contract and receives the entire payment upfront in year one. How much revenue should it recognise in year one?
options: None - wait until all 3 years pass, then recognise it all at once
The full revenue, since the full cash was already received upfront
2/3 of the revenue, with the rest recognised in the final year
1/3 of the revenue, since only 1 of the 3 years is complete
quiz.explanation: The cash received is an advance (deferred revenue). Each year the company completes 1/3 of its obligation, so it recognises 1/3 of the revenue - the same in year 2, and again in year 3.

quiz.question: What is a "performance obligation"?
options: The contract the company must fulfil for the customer (delivering goods, providing a service, and so on)
The company's duty to pay its own upstream suppliers for inputs
A legal requirement dictating how the internal accounting department must be organised
A penalty a company must pay for missing its sales targets
quiz.explanation: A performance obligation is the work the company owes the customer. Each time it completes one obligation, the company may recognise a corresponding slice of revenue.

keyTakeaways: Accrual accounting: recognised once delivery/service is complete
Cash accounting: recognised only when cash is actually received

practicePrompt.question: A software company signs a 120-million-dong-per-year SaaS contract, and the customer pays the full 120 million upfront on the signing date (1 January). By 31 March (end of Q1), how much revenue should the company recognise from this contract?
options: 30 million, because the company has only completed 3 of the 12 months of the service it promised to deliver
120 million - because the customer already paid the full amount upfront, so it's all recognised at once
0 dong - because revenue can only be recognised once the entire contract year has passed
60 million - because half the contract value is always recognised as soon as cash arrives
practicePrompt.explanation: Revenue is recognised according to how much of the obligation is fulfilled, not according to cash flow: by the end of Q1 the company has only delivered 3 of 12 months of service, so it recognises only 30 million in revenue; the remaining 90 million stays as deferred revenue (a liability) until it is 'earned' gradually over the following quarters.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Accrual accounting: recognised once delivery/service is complete

application.title: Find an accrual example in your own work
application.message: Think about your own work or business, or someone you know: is there a transaction that's already complete (goods delivered, work finished) but the cash hasn't arrived yet? Write it down and identify it as accrual revenue.
application.secondary: If you freelance or sell things, an example like this usually turns up in the past month alone.

sections.text: Two companies each sell a batch of goods worth 100 million dong on day 1. One books the revenue immediately on day 1; the other waits until day 30, when the customer pays, before booking it. Who is right? The answer sits in one of accounting's most important principles: accrual.
Accrual accounting: recognised by obligation, not by cash flow

Under the accrual principle that most large businesses follow (and that Vietnamese accounting law requires), revenue is recognised once the business has completed its obligation to deliver goods or provide a service to the customer - regardless of whether cash has arrived. By contrast, cash accounting only recognises revenue when cash actually lands in the account. Small businesses and household enterprises can use cash accounting for its simplicity, but listed companies must use accrual to correctly reflect the economic substance of a transaction.

An important consequence: a company's income statement can look very good - revenue growing, profit positive - while actual cash flow is negative, because customers haven't paid yet. This is exactly why investors always have to read both the income statement and the cash flow statement, never just one.
Accounts receivable - 'revenue not yet turned into cash'

When revenue is recognised but the cash hasn't arrived, the gap sits in Accounts Receivable on the balance sheet - essentially the customer's 'promise to pay'. If receivables grow much faster than revenue, that can be a warning sign: the company is selling well on paper but struggling to collect the actual cash.

items: Cash sales: revenue and cash are recognised at the same time
Credit sales: revenue is recognised immediately, cash arrives later - creating a receivable
Cash collected upfront, delivery later: cash arrives first but revenue isn't recognised yet - creating deferred revenue

left.label: Accrual accounting
left.text: Recognises revenue when the delivery/service obligation is completed. Reflects the true substance of business activity, but can mask cash-flow problems if not read alongside the cash flow statement.

right.label: Cash accounting
right.text: Recognises revenue only when cash actually lands in the account. Simple, suits small household businesses, but doesn't reflect the true scale of activity if the business has many credit transactions.

concepts.def: Recognises revenue/expenses when the obligation arises, regardless of when cash is received/paid.
The amount customers still owe the company after revenue has been recognised.
Cash received in advance but the delivery/service obligation is not yet complete.
A specific commitment the business makes to a customer, and the trigger for recognising revenue.

lines: Revenue is an accounting concept, not a physical stack of cash in a drawer.
Understanding accrual keeps you from confusing 'the company is profitable' with 'the company has cash'.
